questions.question: What does this print?
options: Compile error: String has no shout()
questions.explanation: `fun String.shout()` adds a function that can be called on any `String`. Inside it, `this` is the receiver `"hi"`, so it returns `"HI" + "!"`.

questions.question: Which declaration lets you write `context.toast("Saved")` anywhere you have a `Context`?
options: fun Context.toast(msg: String) = Toast.makeText(this, msg, Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
fun toast(Context.msg: String) = Toast.makeText(this, msg, Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
extension fun Context.toast(msg: String) = Toast.makeText(this, msg, Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
fun Context::toast(msg: String) = Toast.makeText(this, msg, Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
questions.explanation: You declare an extension by putting the receiver type before the function name: `fun Context.toast(...)`. Kotlin has no `extension` keyword, and `::` is for callable references, not declarations.

questions.question: A top-level extension `fun User.debug()` can read `private` properties of `User`.
questions.explanation: An extension is really a static function that takes the receiver as a parameter, so it gets no special access. It can only see the members it could see from outside the class (public, plus internal in the same module).

questions.question: Given this extension, what is `16.dp` on a device whose display density is `2.0`?
options: It doesn't compile, because extension properties need a backing field
questions.explanation: `this` is the receiver `16`, and the getter multiplies it by the density `2.0`, giving `32`. Extension properties have no backing field, which is why they are written with a getter like this one.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Extensions are chosen at compile time from the declared type. `d` is declared as `Dog`, so you get `Woof`. Inside `speak`, the parameter `a` is declared as `Animal`, so `Animal.sound()` runs even though the object is a `Dog`.

questions.question: Which declaration lets `listOf(1, 2).second()` return an `Int` and `listOf("a", "b").second()` return a `String`?
questions.explanation: A generic extension declares its type parameter before the receiver, as in `fun <T> List<T>.second()`, so `T` is inferred for each call. Without `<T>`, the name `T` is undefined, and `List<Any>` would give back `Any` instead of the element type.

questions.question: If `fun View.gone()` is declared in package `com.app.ui.ext`, a file in package `com.app.feature` has to import it (e.g. `import com.app.ui.ext.gone`) before it can call `view.gone()`.
questions.explanation: Top-level extensions are only visible where they are declared or imported, like any other top-level function. You import one by its name, e.g. `import com.app.ui.ext.gone` or `import com.app.ui.ext.*`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: When a member and an extension have the same signature, the member always wins. The extension compiles but can never be called this way (the compiler only warns that it is shadowed).

questions.question: In this extension, what does `view` refer to?
options: The Fragment's own `view`, via the implicit `this` receiver
A parameter that the caller has to pass in
Nothing, because extensions can't access properties of their receiver
questions.explanation: Inside an extension, `this` is the receiver (here the `Fragment`), and its public members can be used without a qualifier. So `view` and `requireContext()` mean `this.view` and `this.requireContext()`.

questions.question: Which of these are real extensions from AndroidX Core KTX (`androidx.core:core-ktx`)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Core KTX provides `SharedPreferences.edit { }`, the `View.isVisible` extension property and `bundleOf(...)`. `toast()` and `gone()` are popular helpers that teams write themselves (or took from the old Anko library), but they aren't part of core-ktx.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: An extension on `String?` can be called on `null` without `?.`. Inside it, `this` is just a nullable value, so nothing throws. Both `null` and `""` count as null-or-empty, so each becomes `-`.

questions.question: Why doesn't this compile?
options: Extension properties have no backing field, so they can't have an initializer
Extension properties must be declared with `var`
`this` can only be used inside extension functions, not in extension property initializers
`Char` isn't allowed as the type of an extension property
questions.explanation: An extension can't add state to a class, so there is nowhere to store an initial value. Write it with a getter instead: `val String.lastChar: Char get() = this[length - 1]`.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Compile error: guest() needs a User instance
Compile error: companion object has no members
questions.explanation: Declaring an extension on `User.Companion` lets you call it like a static factory: `User.guest()`. The class only needs a companion object to exist, even an empty one.

questions.question: This code compiles, and the call in `main` runs the extension.
questions.explanation: The "member wins" rule only applies when the member could handle the call. The member `log` takes one argument, so it can't take `("hi", "UI")`, and the two-argument extension overload is used.

questions.question: `fun String.isEmail(): Boolean` is declared at the top level of `StringUtils.kt`. How do you call it from Java?
questions.explanation: Top-level extensions compile to static methods in a class named after the file plus `Kt`, and the receiver becomes the first parameter. Java can't use receiver syntax, and `INSTANCE` only exists for `object` declarations.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `toString()` can be called on a nullable value because the stdlib declares `fun Any?.toString()`, an extension with a nullable receiver. For `null` it returns the string `"null"`, whose length is 4.

questions.question: What are the types of `a` and `b`?
questions.code:
fun String?.safeLength(): Int = this?.length ?: 0

val s: String? = null
val a = s.safeLength()
val b = s?.safeLength()
options: `b` doesn't compile because the receiver type is already nullable
questions.explanation: `s.safeLength()` always calls the nullable-receiver extension and returns its declared `Int`. Using `?.` is still allowed, but a safe call skips the call when `s` is null and makes the result `Int?`. Here `b` is `null`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Kotlin first looks for a member that can take the call. `put(x: Any)` accepts a `String`, so it wins even though the extension's `String` parameter is a closer match. The extension is only used when no member fits.

questions.question: Given `fun Any.kind() = "any"` and `fun String.kind() = "string"`, which expressions return `"string"`? Select all that apply.
options: val x: Any = "hi"; if (x is String) x.kind()
questions.explanation: The extension is picked from the compile-time type of the expression. After `x is String`, the smart cast makes the type `String`, so `String.kind()` is chosen. The other three have static type `Any` or `CharSequence`, so they get `Any.kind()` even though every value is a `String`.
